title: The Marshmallow Test
sourceNote: Bài viết gốc theo phong cách IELTS Academic Reading; dữ kiện tổng hợp từ các nghiên cứu tâm lý học phát triển đã công bố.

sections.text: Self-control is often described as one of the most valuable qualities a person can possess. It allows us to save money rather than spend it, to study for an examination instead of going out, and to resist the countless small temptations of daily life. For half a century, discussions of this quality have returned again and again to a deceptively simple experiment involving young children and sweets. Known popularly as the marshmallow test, it has been featured in bestselling books, television documentaries and even advertising campaigns, and it has encouraged many parents to wonder what their own children's ability to wait might reveal about their future.

The research began in the late 1960s at a nursery school on the campus of Stanford University, where the psychologist Walter Mischel and his students invited four- and five-year-olds into a small room. Each child was offered a choice between one small reward, such as a marshmallow or a biscuit, which could be eaten immediately, and two rewards if they were willing to wait until the researcher returned. The adult then left the room for up to fifteen minutes. Some children ate the treat almost at once; others managed to hold out for the entire period, and the researchers recorded exactly how long each child was able to wait.

The experiment might have remained a minor study of childhood behaviour had Mischel not stayed in touch with many of the families. Years later, when the children had become teenagers, he and his colleagues sent questionnaires to their parents and gathered information about their academic progress. The results appeared striking. Children who had waited longer in the nursery tended to be described as more competent adolescents, better able to cope with stress, and they had achieved higher scores on university entrance tests. To many observers, it seemed that a few minutes in front of a marshmallow could predict a lifetime of success. The findings, published in a series of papers in the late 1980s and early 1990s, quickly attracted attention far beyond academic psychology.

Mischel was at least as interested in how children waited as in whether they did. Watching through a one-way mirror, his team saw children cover their eyes, sing to themselves, kick the table or turn their chairs away from the tray. In later variations, researchers suggested different ways of thinking about the reward. Children who were encouraged to focus on its abstract qualities, for example by imagining the marshmallows as fluffy white clouds, waited considerably longer than those told to think about how sweet and chewy they would taste. Self-control, these studies implied, was not simply a fixed trait but partly a skill that could be learned.

The original work, however, had an important weakness: almost all of the children were the sons and daughters of Stanford staff and students, a highly educated and relatively wealthy group. In 2018, Tyler Watts and his colleagues repeated the analysis using data on more than nine hundred children from a much more varied range of backgrounds. They did find a link between waiting time at the age of four and academic achievement at fifteen, but it was only about half as strong as the earlier research had suggested. Moreover, once they took into account factors such as family income and the child's early language skills, the connection almost disappeared.

Other researchers have asked why a child might decide not to wait. In a study at the University of Rochester, Celeste Kidd and her colleagues first gave children a set of worn crayons and promised to bring better art materials soon. For half of the children the researcher kept this promise; for the other half she returned empty-handed. When the marshmallow test followed, children who had experienced the broken promise waited only about three minutes on average, while those in the reliable condition waited around twelve. For a child whose experience suggests that adults cannot be trusted, eating the marshmallow straight away may be an entirely rational decision.

Culture appears to matter as well. A study comparing children in Japan and the United States found that Japanese children waited longer when the reward was food, whereas American children waited longer when it was a wrapped present. The researchers linked this to everyday habits: Japanese children are commonly taught to wait until everyone is served before they begin eating, while American children often have to wait for birthdays or holidays to open their gifts. Taken together, these findings suggest that the marshmallow test measures not only a child's willpower but also the circumstances and customs in which that child has grown up.

explain.B: Đoạn B mô tả cách thí nghiệm gốc được dựng: trẻ 4–5 tuổi, chọn một phần thưởng ngay hoặc hai phần nếu chờ, người lớn rời phòng tới 15 phút → tiêu đề {h} (cách thí nghiệm gốc được thiết lập).
explain.C: Đoạn C: nhiều năm sau, trẻ chờ lâu hơn có điểm thi đại học cao hơn, đối phó stress tốt hơn – mối liên hệ 'có vẻ' với thành công về sau → {h}. Chữ 'apparent' khớp với 'The results appeared striking'.
explain.D: Đoạn D: trẻ che mắt, hát, quay ghế đi; nghĩ về kẹo như 'đám mây bông' giúp chờ lâu hơn → các kỹ thuật giúp cưỡng lại cám dỗ: {h}. Đừng chọn {i:6} vì đoạn không khuyên cha mẹ dạy con.
explain.E: Đoạn E: Watts (2018) dùng hơn 900 trẻ với xuất thân đa dạng hơn, mối liên hệ chỉ còn khoảng một nửa và gần như biến mất khi tính đến thu nhập gia đình → mẫu rộng hơn cho kết quả yếu hơn: {h}.
explain.F: Đoạn F: nghiên cứu của Celeste Kidd – trẻ bị thất hứa chỉ chờ khoảng 3 phút, trẻ được giữ lời chờ khoảng 12 phút. Ý chính là người lớn có đáng tin hay không → {h}.
explain.G: Đoạn G: trẻ Nhật chờ lâu hơn với đồ ăn, trẻ Mỹ chờ lâu hơn với quà, do thói quen nuôi dạy ở mỗi nước → {h}. Đoạn có nhắc đồ ăn nhưng không nói chế độ ăn thay đổi nên không phải {i:8}.

items.q: What was the main weakness of Mischel's original research?
options: The children were too young to understand the instructions.
The children came from a narrow social group.
The researchers did not record how long children waited.
Too few parents returned the questionnaires.
items.e: Đoạn E: 'almost all of the children were the sons and daughters of Stanford staff and students, a highly educated and relatively wealthy group' – nhóm xã hội hẹp, khá giả. Bài không nói tỷ lệ phản hồi bảng hỏi thấp.

items.q: Kidd's study suggests that a child who eats the marshmallow immediately
options: may be responding sensibly to past experience.
is likely to have poor language skills.
has probably not understood the choice.
will perform badly in later examinations.
items.e: Đoạn F, câu cuối: với đứa trẻ có kinh nghiệm cho thấy người lớn không đáng tin, ăn kẹo ngay 'may be an entirely rational decision' – phản ứng hợp lý dựa trên trải nghiệm trước đó.

items.q: What is the writer's overall view of the marshmallow test?
options: It is a reliable way of predicting how successful a child will be as an adult.
It is now considered too unreliable to be of any further use to researchers.
It reflects children's environment as well as their willpower.
It proves that self-control is a fixed trait that cannot be taught.
items.e: Đoạn G, câu cuối: bài test đo 'not only a child's willpower but also the circumstances and customs in which that child has grown up' – phản ánh cả môi trường lẫn ý chí. Đoạn D còn cho thấy tự chủ có thể học được.

items.e: Đoạn D: trẻ tưởng tượng kẹo như 'fluffy white clouds' 'waited considerably longer than those told to think about how sweet and chewy they would taste' → chờ lâu hơn những trẻ nghĩ về vị kẹo.

items.e: Đoạn F: trẻ trải qua lời hứa bị thất hứa 'waited only about three minutes on average' → chỉ chờ khoảng ba phút.
